1:
Henry's opening is a maxim: evil manners beget good laws, and evil proverbs beget good prophecies. He allows the saying had occasion. God had declared he would visit the iniquity of fathers on children, chiefly to express his detestation of idolatry; and the prophets had reckoned the sins of earlier kings into the present ruin, the nation being a body politic, and a corporation never dies. What is true in the proverb is that those who eat sour grapes will feel it: the fruit looks well in the temptation and is bitterness itself in the reflection. What is false is the use made of it: they meant a reflection on God's equity, and showed themselves unhumbled under the rod, condemning him and justifying themselves.

Calvin sees the same distortion and is harder on it. Perverse interpreters, he says, always turn heaven's teaching backwards, and the world is full of men who search the law for material to joke with. His parallel is a Latin poet who told the Romans they must bear the vengeance of the gods for crimes not their own until they repaired the temples; Calvin asks why that trifler called his own generation undeserving, when crimes were rife at Rome in his day too. The complaint is a corrupt nature's testimony: we throw the blame as far from ourselves as we can, then quarrel with God's judgments.

Keil and Delitzsch take the wording apart. The verb is not the perfect used by the other prophet who quotes this proverb but an imperfect, fathers eat sour grapes, are accustomed to eat them; and the noun carries no article, since the saying applies to whoever eats them. They also insist the phrase is in the land of Israel rather than concerning it, and name the interpreter they correct. Ellicott agrees, reading it as among the people, those at Jerusalem and those in captivity. Gill and Wesley keep the other sense, taking the proverb to be about the land, and both say the two tribes are meant and not the ten.

Clarke states the question the chapter answers: how far a parent's moral evil extends to his offspring, and whether the faults of parents are not only transferred to children but punished in them. He expects the answer to appear chiefly in another life, when every ligament that now binds societies and nations is dissolved and each bears his own burden; and he notices that the prophet, having a doctrine to settle which touches the comfort of man and the honour of God's government, lays aside his usual figure and allegory and writes with the utmost plainness.

On the oath Gill observes that God swears by his life because he could swear by no greater, which measures how the saying displeased him. Henry notes that the withdrawal of the proverb is a promise elsewhere and a threatening here: there it meant mercy returning, here that their own consciences and their neighbours would confirm they had eaten the same sour grapes, so that shame would silence them. Calvin denies repentance is in view: God means to strike the boasting from under them by making their guilt conspicuous, and they in fact grew more exasperated, not more modest.

The last clause divides them. Gill grounds all souls are mine in creation and reads it as property, dominion and accountability. Calvin knows that reading and refuses it: some make it the potter and the clay, and though that is true in itself, here God is not claiming power but showing fatherly love toward the race he formed, as a workman loves his own work. Ellicott turns it the same way: if all are his, he has no need to punish one lest another escape. He adds that soul here means the person and dying means suffering punishment, where Henry makes the death spiritual and eternal.
5:
Ellicott sets out the shape: general terms at either end, particulars between — religious duties, adultery, then what a man owes his neighbour — the whole a terse summary of practical duty. Keil and Delitzsch call it a picture of the righteousness which has the promise of life, and make it the fulfilling of the law. Calvin describes the same method, a general statement followed by chosen species. Gill will not read it as legal justice, since on those terms no just man exists; he makes it evangelical, resting on imputed righteousness with a principle of grace wrought within, and takes the opening phrase for the inward frame from which the acts proceed. Clarke splits it: holy within, and acting by law and equity.

Eating upon the mountains is idolatry by a figure. Gill notes nothing was unlawful in eating on a mountain as such, only that the temples stood there and the sacrifices were eaten in honour of what they served; Clarke adds that the eating was itself communion with the idol. Calvin presses the point through the apostle, who defines the sin not as bending the knee before wood or stone but by quoting Moses that the people rose up to play after banqueting. Ellicott grants the Lord himself was worshipped in high places against the law, but holds the context points to the sacrificial feasts; on lifting the eyes he suggests any longing short of worship. Calvin makes the eyes the chief outlet of the affections, as a man lifts them to a neighbour's house when he covets it, and weighs the phrase tying the idols to the house of Israel, which shuts off the plea that they abhorred heathen gods while defending ceremonies long in use among the elect.

On the pledge Clarke observes it is generally worth more than the debt, so an unprincipled man finds pretences for keeping it; Ellicott notes borrowing was then the resort of the very poor. Calvin restricts the word to the necessary pledge: a garment, a bed, or the tools a man earns by. A millstone may not be taken, since emptying a poor man's workshop is as good as taking his life; nor may a creditor enter the house to search it, which Calvin calls robbery. Where the text says his bread, Calvin hears the objection that liberality cannot be compelled, and answers that it is yours, yet not so yours that you may refuse a brother whose hunger provokes you to pity. Ellicott says it flatly: these are not optional, and neglecting them is sin.

Usury divides them. Ellicott holds the word means not excessive interest but any interest at all, forbidden of a Hebrew and allowed without limit from a foreigner, a law of kindness rather than a rule of trade. Clarke and Calvin both derive the word from biting, since it gnaws the principal away; Clarke says it bites the receiver in his property and the lender in his salvation, and takes it for exorbitant profit exacted on need. Calvin argues the opposite at length. The law is a complete rule of just living and permitted interest from strangers, so interest cannot be condemned without exception, or the law stands convicted of defect. What must be weighed is the substance, not the word: his own countrymen, finding usury odious, invented a gentler term covering all the old one held. His rule is a borrowed formula — neither everywhere, nor always, nor all things, nor from all. Yet he grants the trade is illiberal, that no well ordered state tolerates a professed usurer, and that a Roman called taking usury much the same as murder.

The promise closes it, and they part. Wesley reads living as deliverance from famine, pestilence and sword, and good days seen. Clarke reads it upward: he has lived to me, and he shall live with me.
10:
Henry takes the wicked son of a good father for the melancholy case it is, and draws the hardest lesson in the chapter from it. Grace does not run in the blood, nor always attend the means of grace; the race is not to the swift, for then well taught children would do well. God will have us know his grace is his own and his Spirit a free agent, and that though we are tied to give our children a good education he is not tied to bless it. Here as much as anywhere appears the power of original sin and the necessity of special grace. Gill says the same in a line, that grace is not conveyed by natural generation though sin is, and finds a name for it: the robber released at the trial was called son of a father, and his own father may have been a good man.

Whether one offence is enough turns on a change of wording. Ellicott observes that the first description is partitive and the second collective, and denies the inference that whoever commits one sin has committed all. The point is that a man who willingly commits any of them puts himself among those who do not intend to abide by God's will but prefer their own, and so ranks himself with God's enemies. Clarke asks it flatly: shall his father's holiness be imputed to him? It shall not. Calvin notices the second catalogue is sharpened: where the first said only that he oppressed a man, this one says the poor and needy, cruelty toward those whose condition should move pity being by so much more atrocious.

Henry allows such a man may prosper a while for his ancestors' piety, but insists his descent will not stand him in stead: it aggravates the sin and the condemnation, and makes the misery afterward less tolerable, not more. Wesley notices that the word for blood in the sentence upon him is plural, and reads two bloods in it: that of the innocent he murdered, and his own, thereby forfeited, so that the whole blame of his misery in time and eternity lies on himself.

The third case reverses the first, and Henry is glad of it: men do not gather grapes of thorns, but God sometimes does, taking a branch from a wild olive and grafting it into a good tree. Where children ordinarily see their parents' sins and do the like, this one sees them and dreads doing the like; he will not publish his father's shame as the mocking son once did, but loathes it, and thinks the worse of sin for its being the ruin of his own house. Clarke has him laying to heart his father's evil life and what it came to. Gill names two kings of Judah who were exactly this, godly sons of idolaters. Keil and Delitzsch put the section under one line: the son who avoids his father's sin will live, and the father will die for his own.

Calvin turns the third case against the proverb. If sons really suffered for what their fathers ate, godly men descended from despisers of God would be clear of all their own sins, and a good king would have borne the punishment due his idolatrous father. Ellicott uses it the same way: here at last was a father who had eaten sour grapes, and the son's teeth were not set on edge. Calvin adds that the quarrel was never about the right but about the fact, since nobody argued that God ought to spare the innocent; they were so possessed by the error that punishment overruns the guilty they could not see justice is never robbed of its reward. Clarke closes with an even balance: he is no more affected by his father's crimes than his father was benefited by his grandfather's righteousness.
19:
Ellicott reads the people's interruption as one question rather than two, and takes it seriously. It seemed to them the law of nature and the teaching of history that a son should bear his father's iniquity; their ideas had not risen to individual responsibility, the individual being still only part of a family or a nation, and they wanted to know why a universal law was reversed. His answer is that none was reversed, only that a higher law prevailed over a lower; and the divine word, he observes, does not argue with the objection but says the thing again. Gill hears blasphemy in it, a quarrel with the prophet and with God over what they claim to feel every day.

Calvin faces the harder form of it, since God so often declares that he visits the iniquity of fathers upon children to the third and fourth generation. He answers in two moves. First, nobody dies innocent. The whole race fell in one man, so the curse is partly another's and partly our own; a child is corrupt before birth, and though nothing shows in infancy the corruption is rightly reckoned sin before a sight keener than ours, which is why a psalmist reminded of one sin went back to his conception. Second, the penalty on the children of the impious is chiefly inward. Sword, famine and pestilence are visible; the hidden penalty is that God withdraws the spirit of rectitude, gives them up to a reprobate mind, and leaves them in the death they were born in.

Wesley resolves it another way. Could we see the connexions between persons and between sins, and how easily and undiscerned men come to share the same sins, we should find father and son both guilty, neither punished beyond his own account. Scripture dooms nobody for sins he is wholly free of; and the promise, as he glosses it, is that the son shall not die eternally for his father's iniquity if he does not tread in its steps, nor the father for the son's.

Clarke marks the turn: the simple cases are done and two remain, the wicked man who repents and the righteous man who backslides. Ellicott adds the architecture: the second is the briefer, since the object is to encourage hope in repentance, and the pair is repeated in reverse order for emphasis.

What counts as turning is defined narrowly. Henry makes consideration the first step, since sinners go on precisely because they never consider the end of it; the aversion must be universal, no reserve kept for one favourite sin, because we do not hate sin as sin unless we hate all of it; and it must be joined to obedience, on God's rule and not the world's. Calvin arrives from the other side. Many make a half conversion and think themselves safe, mingling virtues with vices and reckoning the guilt cancelled if they can produce something creditable, which is like serving a master muddy wine mixed with filth as well as dregs. Conversion begins when a man renounces himself, and is not conversion till he gives himself to obedience.

Then the forgetting. Clarke says the transgressions are so completely forgiven they will not even be mentioned to him; Wesley narrows the phrase to exactly that, not mentioned to him. Calvin calls it a voluntary oblivion by which the penitent pass at once out of death into life, God being unable to be entreated while he imputes. Ellicott admits an apparent contradiction, that a forgiven man is seen to suffer all his life from what he did, one king's whole reign lying under a cloud after his great sin. The natural consequences are not cancelled but run in subservience to a higher moral law, and the man's present state decides whether they will be, painful as they are, for his highest gain.
23:
Ellicott makes the question about God's pleasure the fundamental truth under both testaments. God created man, and when he had fallen ordered both dispensations and used methods of infinite love to win him back; his delight can only be in a creature fulfilling the design it was made for. Yet neither, the next verse declares, can he suffer his love to be set at nought. Calvin says God desires nothing more earnestly than that those rushing to destruction should turn back. Even the heathen, without law or prophets and suffocated by errors, were moved by a secret impulse to seek pardon, as though the sense that God may be appeased by seekers were born in them.

Gill will not take the denial absolutely. God does take pleasure in these judgments so far as they fulfil his word, secure the honour of his truth, glorify his justice and above all reclaim men; the denial is comparative, mercy being his delight and destruction his strange work. Clarke reads it absolutely and draws from it a conclusion about decrees. God can do nothing with which he is not pleased, and so can decree nothing with which he is not pleased; since he is not pleased with the death of a sinner, he cannot have decreed to abandon a man to the evil of his nature and then condemn him for what he could not avoid.

The righteous man who falls away raises the sharpest disagreement in the chapter, over what righteousness is lost. Gill denies it can be a truly righteous man, since nobody is righteous by anything of his own but by an imputed righteousness which is God's and can never be lost; the man in view is righteous in his own esteem and his neighbours' account, holding a ceremonial or at best a merely moral righteousness. Clarke names that reading and rejects it as the gloss of theologians. God never speaks of turning from self-righteousness, which in his eyes is a nonentity; there is no holiness but what he infuses, so what is meant is a real righteous principle and practice, and a man once holy may fall from it and perish everlastingly. Calvin stands nearer Clarke, warning the man who thinks he stands, and holding that only perseverance is blessed, a temporary righteousness never profiting an apostate.

Calvin insists the two halves belong together: God invites the perishing with open arms, and by the other clause keeps the confident within bounds. He puts the case as a question: if God absolves those who repent and condemns the just man who abandons a holy course, what is left to complain of? Ellicott qualifies the place where the text speaks of a man saving his own soul alive. It does not mean anyone saves himself by his own power, a question not in view, but that this course of conduct has salvation for its consequence, and that taking it lies within the man's choice.

The complaint returns twice, and they treat it as escalation. Ellicott notes the word means literally weighed out or balanced: the charge is that God is arbitrary, the reply that he rewards and punishes by immutable principles, every man reaping what he sowed. Wesley takes the way for God's whole management of affairs, and the charge to be that it does not square with his declared law. Gill, listing how many ways the case had been put, calls the repetition stubbornness rather than blindness. Calvin describes the progress. Hypocrites begin by finding fault indirectly and pretending they do not, accusing God of rigour in the act of excusing themselves; then, gaining nothing by the double dealing, they are inflamed to condemn him outright. His last word is that no virtue is approved without perseverance, and that men are never so rash as when they curse God while their own ways are the crooked ones.
30:
Henry frames the close as a verdict. After a fair trial at the bar of right reason the finding is for God, his ways are equal, and judgment should follow; one would expect a sentence of condemnation. Instead comes a miracle of mercy, the day of grace lengthened out, the whole ending in a call to repent with a promise of pardon attached. Calvin hears authority in the judging clause: plead as you please, I settle the strife in a word, since each of you is judged by my will; and though you will not own yourselves worthy of destruction, it is enough that the lawful judge pronounces it. Gill has the case fairly stated and the charge removed, so sentence may pass.

Henry counts four duties in the exhortation and finds an image for each. Turn from sin, and turn against it as an enemy you loathe; abandon it with a resolution never to return, giving it a bill of divorce, breaking every league made with it, throwing it overboard as the mariners threw the runaway prophet who raised the storm, and crucifying it as a malefactor. Clarke asks the same violence, dashing away every incentive along with the act. Gill reads the casting away of the transgressions as the casting away of their idols, though he records a Jewish commentator taking it of the punishment, which repentance might escape.

The command to make a new heart is the hard place, and all of them see it. Calvin says men badly trained in Scripture erect their crests on this verse as though conversion lay in free will, concluding either that the exhortation is a deceit or that the alienated can return by their own motion. His answer is that when God shows the elect a duty they know they cannot discharge, they fly to the Spirit for help, so the exhortation becomes the instrument by which the grace is conferred; and he rests on an old prayer: grant what you command, and command what you wish. Henry says it plainly: God does not command what cannot be done, but bids us do what is in our power and pray for what is not. Clarke has the asking do the work: call on God and he will give it, and because you ask, he is pleased in some sort to attribute to you what his grace alone performs. Ellicott denies human sufficiency is in question at all: the new heart can be no one's work but the Spirit's, yet the Spirit is given to those who ask, and the decision still falls to each man.

Calvin also separates the two words: the heart is the will and the seat of the affections, the spirit the intellectual part. Since nothing less than a renewal of both would reconcile these people, he concludes that nothing in us is sound, and an entire renovation is needed before we can please God.

Clarke takes the closing question apart word by word. Why: name one reason. Will: nothing but obstinacy, or a voluntary listlessness about salvation, can prevent you. Ye: children of many mercies, fed all your life, redeemed, who promised to renounce the pomps of the world. Henry reaches the same point: sinners die because they will die, going down the road to death and never coming up to the terms on which life is offered. On the last denial Gill again reads comparatively, taking the death for calamity and captivity and the wish for their repenting and living on in their own land. Clarke reads perdition, and adds that no one is damned for a fallen nature, only for refusing the grace that pardons it; and since no man has more grace than will save himself, a parent's righteousness assists nobody. Wesley reduces it to a line: sinners displease God when they undo themselves, and please him when they return.
